# Platform-service development mocks

## Summary

SystemHost declarations will model shared platform services as external Dapr app identities used by individual integration components. An optional, separate development definition will resolve selected services to OpenAPI-backed mocks. During local SystemHost runs, one Microcks instance will host those mocks and generated Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` resources will transparently redirect existing service-invocation calls to Microcks.

Integration projects, platform-service implementations, client configuration, and production Dapr app IDs remain unchanged.

## Context

Intropy integration components use Dapr service invocation to call two shared platform services:

- `idempotency-service`
- `business-incident-service`

The inspected order-flow system confirms the relevant behavior:

- both `order-extractor` and `order-loader` use both services;
- both components retain the client packages' default Dapr app IDs;
- the framework calls `POST /status` and `POST /commit` on the idempotency service;
- the framework calls `POST /events` with structured CloudEvents to trigger or resolve business incidents;
- each component already carries local `HTTPEndpoint` resources with the production app IDs as `metadata.name` values;
- those endpoints currently target locally hosted real services with their databases, messaging, migrations, and Dapr sidecars.

The existing component overlay gives the SystemHost a clean substitution point: generated resources replace component-local resources with the same `metadata.name` when staging each sidecar's effective Dapr resource set.

Dapr resolves a named `HTTPEndpoint` before app-ID discovery. A development resource named `idempotency-service` therefore satisfies an unchanged invocation of `/v1.0/invoke/idempotency-service/method/status` while forwarding it to Microcks.

## Goals

- Make platform-service dependencies visible in the topology.
- Preserve existing integration code, client configuration, and service invocation paths.
- Scope each generated mock endpoint to the components that declared the dependency.
- Keep development substitutions separate from the environment-independent system topology.
- Run one lightweight Microcks instance for all declared OpenAPI mocks.
- Keep mock behavior stateless and contract-backed in the first version.
- Preserve deterministic generation and the existing component-overlay model.
- Fail before integration startup when a declared mock cannot be imported or addressed.

## Non-goals

- Deploying the real platform services.
- Changing either platform service or its client package.
- Stateful idempotency behavior, duplicate history, or incident lifecycle emulation.
- Scenario switching, latency injection, or failure injection.
- Falling back from a mock to a real service.
- Mocking Dapr pub/sub, bindings, or arbitrary external systems.
- Replacing standalone component development commands; they continue using their own local Dapr resources unless addressed separately.
- Generating Kubernetes workloads for platform services or Microcks.

## Design principles

### Dependencies are identities

A platform-service dependency is identified by the Dapr app ID that callers already invoke. It does not contain an image, port, Helm chart, or local implementation.

### Usage is component-scoped

Dependencies are edges from a component to an external platform service. Per-component declarations support accurate topology graphs, narrow Dapr scopes, and startup dependencies without coupling unrelated components.

### Development resolution is separate

The system topology records that a component uses a service. An optional development definition records that local runs resolve that service to an OpenAPI mock. Microcks remains an Aspire implementation detail rather than part of the core DSL vocabulary.

### The adapter is unnecessary

A Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` already preserves the caller-facing service invocation API and can contain the full Microcks service/version base path. A proxy adapter would add processes, sidecars, readiness, and forwarding semantics without changing the result.

## Proposed DSL

### Platform-service references

SystemHosts declare reusable service references alongside topics and connectors:

```csharp
using Intropy.Topology;

public static class Services
{
    public static readonly ServiceRef Idempotency =
        ServiceRef.Define("idempotency-service");

    public static readonly ServiceRef BusinessIncidents =
        ServiceRef.Define("business-incident-service");
}
```

`ServiceRef` contains one value: `AppId`. The value is validated as a DNS-1123 label when the reference is created.

### Component usage

Every component builder exposes `.Uses(ServiceRef)` and returns its concrete builder type:

```csharp
public void Define(SystemBuilder builder)
{
    builder.AddExtractor("order-extractor")
        .From(Connectors.OrderExtractorSource)
        .Publishes(Topics.Order)
        .Uses(Services.Idempotency)
        .Uses(Services.BusinessIncidents)
        .WithSchedule("* * * * *");

    builder.AddLoader("order-loader")
        .Subscribes(Topics.Order)
        .To(Connectors.OrderLoaderDestination)
        .Uses(Services.Idempotency)
        .Uses(Services.BusinessIncidents);
}
```

The declaration describes connectivity only. It does not imply that the SystemHost owns or deploys the provider.

### Separate development definition

Development substitutions live in a separate discoverable type:

```csharp
using Intropy.Topology.Generation;

public sealed class OrderFlowDevelopment : IDevelopmentDefinition
{
    public void Define(DevelopmentBuilder development)
    {
        development.Mock(Services.Idempotency)
            .FromOpenApi("mocks/idempotency-service.openapi.yaml");

        development.Mock(Services.BusinessIncidents)
            .FromOpenApi("mocks/business-incident-service.openapi.yaml");
    }
}
```

Artifact paths are relative to the SystemHost directory. OpenAPI `info.title` and `info.version` determine the Microcks service identity and URL. The DSL does not repeat those values.

The expected SystemHost layout is:

```text
order-flow/
├── OrderFlowSystem.cs
├── OrderFlowDevelopment.cs
├── Services.cs
└── mocks/
    ├── idempotency-service.openapi.yaml
    └── business-incident-service.openapi.yaml
```

## Core topology model

`ServiceRef` belongs to `Intropy.Topology` because service usage is part of the environment-independent topology.

Conceptually, each materialized component gains its used app IDs:

```csharp
public sealed record ComponentModel
{
    public required IReadOnlyList<string> Uses { get; init; }
}
```

The topology also exposes resources derived from those edges:

```csharp
public sealed record ServiceResource
{
    public required string AppId { get; init; }
    public required IReadOnlyList<string> Consumers { get; init; }
}
```

`SystemTopology.Services` is sorted by app ID. `Consumers` is unique and sorted. Component declaration order remains unchanged.

As with topics and connectors, service resources materialize from usage. There is no system-level `AddService` or `UsesService` method.

## Development model and discovery

Development types belong to `Intropy.Topology.Generation`, keeping Microcks and local-runtime concerns out of the core topology package.

The generation package provides:

- `IDevelopmentDefinition`
- `DevelopmentBuilder`
- an immutable development manifest
- development-definition discovery
- validation of mock declarations and artifacts

Discovery rules:

1. The assembly must still contain exactly one `ISystemDefinition`.
2. The assembly may contain zero or one concrete `IDevelopmentDefinition`.
3. The system topology is built before the development definition.
4. The development builder receives the validated topology so it can reject unknown or unused service references.
5. No development definition means no generated service mocks and no Microcks resource.

The separate development type keeps generated or regenerated system declarations focused on topology and lets local configuration evolve independently.

## OpenAPI contract handling

The development manifest records the service app ID and resolved artifact path. Contract inspection extracts:

- OpenAPI version;
- `info.title`;
- `info.version`.

The development tooling supports the OpenAPI versions supported by the pinned Microcks release. Missing or unreadable identity fields fail validation.

Microcks URLs are built in one internal abstraction from the imported identity. SystemHost authors do not encode Microcks paths or title escaping.

The first order-flow mock contracts are deliberately narrow overlays matching actual client traffic rather than copies of the full upstream API documents.

### Idempotency mock

Required operations:

```text
POST /status → 200
{"action":"Proceed","reason":"NoPreviousData"}

POST /commit → 200 with an empty body
```

The mock always allows processing and accepts every commit. It does not retain state.

### Business-incident mock

Required operation:

```text
POST /events → 202 with an empty body
Content-Type: application/cloudevents+json
```

The same operation accepts triggered and resolved structured CloudEvents. The mock does not persist or expose incidents.

Each operation includes the OpenAPI examples and Microcks associations required to produce a response, including `x-microcks-refs` where a bodyless response needs an explicit request-example association.

## Generated Dapr resources

Generation accepts the validated topology and optional development manifest. It emits one `HTTPEndpoint` for each mocked service.

Conceptually:

```yaml
apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: HTTPEndpoint
metadata:
  name: idempotency-service
spec:
  baseUrl: http://localhost:8585/rest/<encoded-title>/<encoded-version>
scopes:
- order-extractor
- order-loader
```

Generation rules:

- `metadata.name` is the service app ID.
- `spec.baseUrl` is derived from the imported OpenAPI identity.
- `scopes` contains exactly the service's consumers, sorted ordinally.
- Output is deterministic and one resource is emitted per mocked service.
- An unmocked service emits no `HTTPEndpoint`; normal Dapr discovery or a component-local resource remains in effect.
- A generated endpoint replaces a component-local endpoint with the same `metadata.name` during staging.
- Mock resources are part of the local generation profile only and must not appear in production Kubernetes output.

The current `generate` command emits local-run artifacts. When a development definition exists, its generated endpoints are included so command output and Aspire staging use the same generated truth.

## Aspire lifecycle

The Aspire backend starts Microcks only when at least one mock is declared.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C[Discover and validate topology] --> D[Discover and validate development definition]
    D --> G[Generate Dapr resources]
    D --> M[Start one Microcks instance]
    M --> I[Import OpenAPI artifacts]
    I --> V[Verify imported service identities]
    G --> S[Stage per-component Dapr overlays]
    V --> R[Mark mock backend ready]
    S --> A[Start scoped integration sidecars and apps]
    R --> A
```

Lifecycle requirements:

1. Microcks uses one pinned image version and one fixed host endpoint known to generated Dapr resources.
2. Container health is necessary but not sufficient; readiness also requires every declared artifact to be imported and addressable.
3. Only components consuming a mocked service depend on Microcks readiness.
4. Their Dapr sidecars are held before startup until Microcks and contract import are ready.
5. Sidecar recovery uses the same aggregate backend-readiness gate.
6. Scheduled components use the same readiness gate on initial and subsequent starts.
7. Import or verification failure stops the run with the service app ID and artifact path in the error.
8. The Aspire dashboard exposes Microcks as one infrastructure resource.

The fixed port is checked before startup and produces a focused error when unavailable. Port configurability is deferred until there is a demonstrated conflict that cannot be handled operationally.

## CLI behavior

### `check`

- Validates the system topology.
- Discovers and validates the optional development definition.
- Verifies artifact existence and OpenAPI identity without starting Microcks.

### `graph`

- Includes service usage in the environment-independent topology graph.
- Does not include development mock paths or Microcks details.

A component entry lists its used service app IDs, and the graph's resource projection lists each service and its consumers.

### `generate`

- Generates the existing local Dapr resources and runtime configuration.
- Includes development `HTTPEndpoint` resources when a development definition exists.
- Does not start Microcks or import artifacts.

### `run`

- Performs all checks above.
- Starts Microcks, imports and verifies contracts, stages generated endpoints, and then starts consumers.

`Program.cs` remains unchanged because both backends continue discovering definitions from the SystemHost assembly.

## Validation

### Topology validation

- Service app IDs must be valid DNS-1123 labels.
- A component cannot use the same service more than once.
- Service consumers must be declared topology components.
- A service app ID cannot collide with a topology component app ID.
- Service resources must have at least one consumer by construction.

### Development validation

- At most one development definition may exist.
- A mocked service must occur in the built topology.
- A service may have at most one mock declaration.
- A mock artifact path must resolve within or beneath the SystemHost directory; escaping through `..` is rejected.
- The artifact must exist, be readable, and contain a supported OpenAPI document with non-empty title and version.
- Two different mocked services cannot accidentally resolve to the same Microcks service identity unless explicit aliasing is designed later.
- A development definition may leave a used service unmocked; existing Dapr discovery or component-local resources remain valid resolution mechanisms.

Validation messages identify the component or service app ID and the conflicting declaration. No new public diagnostic-code scheme is introduced by this design.

## Compatibility and migration

The feature is additive:

- integration source code does not change;
- client package registration does not change;
- platform-service source code does not change;
- production app IDs do not change;
- existing component-local Dapr resources remain valid for standalone runs;
- SystemHosts without service declarations or development definitions behave as before.

For order-flow, generated mock endpoints use the same names as the existing local endpoints. The established overlay rule replaces those files only during SystemHost runs. Standalone component runs continue targeting the real local services until a separate standalone-development design is adopted.

## Testing strategy

### Core topology tests

- Every component builder supports fluent `.Uses`.
- Usage materializes deterministic component edges and service resources.
- Duplicate usage and app-ID collisions fail validation.
- Graph serialization includes services and consumers without development data.

### Development discovery tests

- Zero or one development definition is accepted.
- Multiple definitions fail with their type names.
- Unknown, unused, duplicate, missing, escaping, and malformed artifacts fail clearly.
- OpenAPI title and version are extracted from supported 3.0 and 3.1 documents.

### Generation tests

- Exact `HTTPEndpoint` YAML snapshots cover name, base URL, escaping, scopes, and ordering.
- Unmocked services produce no endpoint.
- Generated endpoints replace component-local resources by `metadata.name` during staging.
- Repeated generation is byte-identical.

### Aspire model tests

- No mocks means no Microcks resource or readiness dependency.
- Multiple mocks share one Microcks resource.
- Only consumers wait for Microcks.
- Consumer sidecars are gated on contract-import readiness.
- Import failures prevent component startup.
- Scheduled sidecar restarts retain the readiness gate.

### Live compatibility test

An opt-in integration test runs the published platform-service clients through real Dapr sidecars against Microcks and proves:

- idempotency status deserializes to `Proceed / NoPreviousData`;
- commit receives an empty `200`;
- triggered and resolved structured CloudEvents receive `202`;
- integration code and app-ID configuration remain unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

- The order-flow SystemHost can run both components without starting either real platform service or its backing infrastructure.
- Existing invocations to `idempotency-service` and `business-incident-service` succeed through Dapr without integration changes.
- The generated endpoints are scoped to `order-extractor` and `order-loader`.
- A valid order flows through extractor and loader with stateless idempotency responses.
- A validation failure can be routed to the business-incident mock and acknowledged successfully.
- Missing or invalid contracts fail before either integration starts.
- SystemHosts without development mocks retain current behavior.

## Alternatives considered

### Dapr-enabled proxy adapters

Rejected for the first version. They preserve app IDs but add one process and sidecar per service, proxy correctness, and additional readiness concerns. `HTTPEndpoint` provides the required transparent substitution directly.

### System-wide service declarations

Rejected. They hide actual consumers, broaden Dapr scopes, and couple unrelated components to mock readiness.

### Manual endpoint YAML in every component

Rejected as the SystemHost solution. Order-flow demonstrates that it works technically, but it duplicates environment configuration across components and cannot centrally import or gate contracts.

### Microcks-specific DSL

Rejected. The declaration should express an OpenAPI-backed mock; the Aspire backend currently fulfils it with Microcks. This keeps tool choice out of the topology surface.

### Full upstream contracts

Rejected for the first version. The inspected upstream artifacts contain operations not used by order-flow and do not fully represent the client traffic needed here. Narrow mock overlays are easier to verify and maintain.

## Risks and mitigations

- **Microcks URL conventions may change.** Keep URL construction in one internal abstraction and pin the Microcks version.
- **OpenAPI mocks may drift from released clients.** Exercise the published clients in an opt-in Dapr/Microcks compatibility test.
- **A mock may conceal a broken production operation.** Keep mocks limited to known client traffic and do not claim production-service conformance from local mock success.
- **Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` remains a `v1alpha1` resource.** Pin and test the supported Dapr runtime range.
- **A fixed Microcks port may collide locally.** Check it before building the Aspire graph and report a focused remediation.
- **Contract import can lag behind container health.** Gate consumers on verified artifact availability, not container state alone.

## Planning handoff

Implementation planning should determine:

- the exact public type locations and names within existing package boundaries;
- the OpenAPI parsing dependency and supported document versions;
- the pinned Microcks integration package and image versions from current official documentation;
- the import/verification mechanism exposed by that Microcks version;
- how aggregate backend readiness is represented without coupling it specifically to Redis or Microcks;
- the exact topology graph wire-format evolution and compatibility policy;
- whether the live Dapr/Microcks test runs in regular CI or an opt-in compatibility lane.

These choices must preserve the DSL, lifecycle, scope boundaries, and observable behavior defined above.

## References

- [Dapr: invoke non-Dapr endpoints](https://docs.dapr.io/developing-applications/building-blocks/service-invocation/howto-invoke-non-dapr-endpoints/)
- [Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` specification](https://docs.dapr.io/reference/resource-specs/httpendpoints-schema/)
- [Microcks OpenAPI conventions](https://microcks.io/documentation/references/artifacts/openapi-conventions/)
- [Microcks dispatching rules](https://microcks.io/documentation/explanations/dispatching/)

Then, it directly discover service definition as well as request/response samples defined as OpenAPI examples. urls.title: Your 1st REST mock
urls.content:
This tutorial is a step-by-step walkthrough on how to use OpenAPI v3 Specification to specify your mocks for your API. This is hands-on introduction to OpenAPI Conventions reference that brings all details on conventions being used.
...
First mandatory step is obviously to setup Microcks 😉. For OpenAPI usage, we don’t need any particular setup and the simple`docker` way of deploying Microcks as exposed in Getting started is perfectly suited. Following the getting started, you should have a Microcks running instance on`http://localhost:8585`.
...
We’re going to add OpenAPI Example Objects. As this operation does not expect anything as input but just produces a result, we’ll add an example called`my_pets` in the response content. Just paste the content below at the end of above skeleton:
...
```
paths:
  /my/pets:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/Pet'
              examples:
                my_pets:
                  value:
                    - id: 1
                      name: Zaza
                    - id: 2
                      name: Tigress
                    - id: 3
                      name: Maki
                    - id: 4
                      name: Toufik
...
As soon as your contract contains examples, you can import it into Microcks and it will use examples to produce real life simulation of your API. Use the Direct Upload method to inject your OpenAPI file in Microcks. You should get the following result:
...
Microcks has found`my_pets` as a valid sample to build a simulation upon. A mock URL has been made available and you can use it to test the API operation as demonstrated below with a`curl` command:
...
`GET` operation in your API, bound to the`/pets` path. Of course, we’ll have to define the`filter` parameter that will be present in query so that users will query`/pets?filter=zoe` to get all the pets having`zoe` in name.
...
So we’ll add a new path snippet in the`paths` section of our OpenAPI document like below. This snippet is also integrating Example Objects for both the query parameter and the response.
...
```
paths:
  [...]
  /pets:
    get:
      parameters:
        - name: filter
          in: query
          schema:
            type: string
          examples:
            k_pets:
              value: k  
      responses:
        "200":
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                type: array
                items:
                  $ref: '#/components/schemas/Pet'
              examples:
                k_pets:
                  value:
                    - id: 3
                      name: Maki
                    - id: 4
                      name: Toufik
...
The important things to notice here is the logic behind example naming. In fact, OpenAPI specification allows to specify example fragments for each and every piece of a contract. To be tied together by Microcks, related parts must have the same key. Here the key is`k_pets` that allows to link`filter=k` with the associated response containing the 2 cats having a`k` in their name. When imported into Microcks, you should have following result:
...
What about dispatching properties we mentioned earlier? You can see that they now having values. Because of the presence of parameter in your operation, Microcks has inferred a routing logic named`URI_PARAMS` that will be based on matching rule on`filter` parameter. Let’s try the mock URL with this command:
...
Another very common construction in OpenAPI is the usage of path parameters. Such parameters are directly integrated into API request URL path so that you have the ability to access identified resources. Typically with the Petstore API, you’d want to allow users to use directly the`/pets/1` to access the cat with identifier`1`.
...
Let’s add such a new operation into the API by adding the following path snippet into the`paths` section. Once again, we’re integrating Example Objects for both the path parameter and the response.
...
```
paths:
  [...]
  /pets/{id}:
    get:
      parameters:
        - name: id
          in: path
          schema:
            type: string
          examples:
            pet_1:
              value: '1'
            pet_2:
              value: '2'
      responses:
        "200":
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Pet'
              examples:
                pet_1:
                  value:
                    id: 1
                    name: Zaza
                pet_2:
                  value:
                    id: 2
                    name: Tigresse
...
The`Dispatcher` inferred by Microcks has been adapted to`URI_PARTS` which means that routing logic is made of parts (or path elements) or the URI. The element that is considered for routing is the`id` parameter. Let’s tests these new mocks with some commands:
...
💡 Microcks dispatcher can support multiple path elements to find appropriate response to an incoming request. In that case, the dispatcher rule will have the form of`part_1 && part_2 && part_3`. In that case of having multiple parts, you may find it useful to reuse definition of example values using`$ref` notation. This is totally supported by Microcks.
...
And now the final step! Let’s deal with a new operation that allows registering a new pet within the Petstore. For that, you’ll typically have to define a new`POST` operation on the`/pets` path. In order to be meaningful to the user of this operation, a mock would have to integrate some logic that reuse contents from the incoming request and/or generate sample data. That’s typically what we’re going to do in this last section 😉
...
Let’s add such a new operation into the API by adding the following path snippet into the`paths/pets` section. The subtlety here is that we’re integrating specific elements in our Example Objects:
...
```
paths:
  /pets:
    [...]
    post:
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/NewPet'
            examples:
              new_pet:
                value:
                  name: Jojo
      responses:
        "201":
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Pet'
              examples:
                new_pet:
                  value: |-
                    {
                      "id": {{ randomInt(5,10) }},
                      "name": "{{ request.body/name }}"
                    }

```
...
Microcks has this ability to generate dynamic mock content. The`new_pet` example fragment above embeds two specific notations that are:
...
- `{{ randomInt(5,10) }}` for asking Microcks to generate a random integer between 5 and 10 for us (remember: the other pets have ids going from 1 to 4),
- `{{ request.body/name }}` for asking Microcks to reuse here the`name` property of the request body. Simply.
...
You can see in the picture above that the`Dispatcher` has no value as we have no parameters in operation. But this does not prevent use to use both parameters and template functions. In fact, template also allows you to reuse response parameters to inject in response content. Let’s now finally test this mock URL using some content and see what’s going on:
...
```
curl http://localhost:8585/rest/Petstore+API/1.0.0/pets -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Rusty"}' -s | jq

```
...
🛠️ As a validation, send a few more requests changing your pet name. You’ll check that given name is always returned. But you can also go further by defining an advanced dispatcher that will inspect your request body content to decide which response must be sent back. Very useful to describe different creation or error cases!

urls.title: API Metadata Format
urls.content:
Some Microcks mocks specific metadata or properties cannot be fully deduced from common attributes coming from OpenAPI or AsyncAPI. Thus we should rely on default values can be later overwritten by`manager` within Microcks either using the UI or through the Microcks API.
...
💡 For OpenAPI and AsyncAPI, we introduced OpenAPI extensions and AsyncAPI extensions to allow providing this informations using`x-microcks` properties.
...
But sometimes you don’t want to add some`x-microcks` extensions attributes into AsyncAPI / OpenAPI document OR you’d need to specify these metadata and properties for some other artifact types like Protobuf+ Postman Collection for GRPC mocking for instance 😉.
...
Hence we propose defining these metadata and properties into a standalone document called an`APIMetadata`; document that can imported as a`secondary` artifact thanks to the Multi-Artifacts support.
...
`APIMetadata` documents are intended to be imported as`secondary` artifacts only ; thanks to the Multi-Artifacts support.
...
Let start with an example! Here’s below an illustration of what could such an`APIMetadata` document for one API. If you’re a reader of the Microcks Blog, you’ll notice this sample API with custom dispatching rules was introduced into the Advanced Dispatching and Constraints for mocks post.
...
```
apiVersion: mocks.microcks.io/v1alpha1
kind: APIMetadata
metadata:
  name: WeatherForecast API
  version: 1.1.0
  labels:
    domain: weather
    status: GA
    team: Team C
operations:
  'GET /forecast/{region}':
    delay: 100
    dispatcher: FALLBACK
    dispatcherRules: |-
      {
        "dispatcher": "URI_PARTS",
        "dispatcherRules": "region",
        "fallback": "Unknown"
      }

```
...
- This document is related to the`WeatherForecast API` in version`1.1.0`. That means that this API version should already exist into your repository, otherwise the document will be ignored,
- This document specifies additional`labels` used for Organizing the Microcks repository. This labels will be added to existing ones,
- This document specifies a default`delay` as well as custom dispatching informations for our`GET` operation. The name of operation should perfectly match the name of an existing operation - whether defined through OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, Postman Collection, SoapUI Project or Protobuf definition - otherwise it will be ignored.
...
💡 Note that we can use multi-line notation in YAML but we will have to escape everything and put`\` before double-quotes and`\n` characters if specified using JSON.
...
The semantic of those attributes are exactly the same that the one introduced into
...
extensions and AsyncAPI extensions.
...
Starting with Microcks`1.11.0`, you can also declare mock constraints into your`APIMetadata` file:
...
```
apiVersion: mocks.microcks.io/v1alpha1
kind: APIMetadata
metadata:
  name: WeatherForecast API
  version: 1.1.0
  labels:
    domain: weather
    status: GA
    team: Team C
...
operations:
  'GET /forecast/{region}':
    delay: 100
    parameterConstraints:
      - name: Authorization
        in: header
        required: true
        recopy: false
        mustMatchRegexp: "^Bearer\\s[a-zA-Z0-9\\._-]+$"
      - name: x-request-id
        in: header
        required: true
        recopy: true

```
...
## Importing API Metadata
...
When you’re happy with your API Metadata just put the result YAML or JSON file into your favorite Source Configuration Management tool, grab the URL of the file corresponding to the branch you want to use and add it as a regular Job import into Microcks. On import, Microcks should detect that it’s an`APIMetadata` specification file and choose the correct importer.

This guide will show you and discuss the different options for importing Services and APIs into Microcks. There are basically two different ways of putting new content into Microcks:

After choosing your artifacts, click the green`Upload` button to send them to Microcks. Notification messages will appear in the top-right corner to inform you of the process. Newly discovered Services and APIs can be found in the APIs | Services repository.
...
### Via the API
...
The same thing can be done via Microcks’ own API. Be sure to start by reading the Connecting to Microcks API guide, and to retrieve a`token` by running the authentication flow. The Service Account you use for this operation is required to have the`manager` role, which is not the case with the default one, as explained in Inspecting default Service Account.
...
Once you have the`$TOKEN` issued for the correct account, uploading a new Artifact is just a matter of executing this`curl` command:

```
# Uploading a local artifact.
curl 'https://microcks.example.com/api/artifact/upload?mainArtifact=true' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -F 'file=@samples/films.graphql' -k

```
...
Direct upload is straightforward and quick to implement, but it has one caveat: it does not automatically resolve dependencies. For example, if your artifact file uses external references with relative paths, Microcks cannot resolve them by default.
...
As a workaround to this limitation, and since Microcks`1.10.1`, we introduced a new`default-artifacts-repository.url` property that takes the value of`DEFAULT_ARTIFACTS_REPOSITORY_URL` environment variable when defined. It can be set to either an HTTP endpoint (starting with`http[s]://`) or a file endpoint (starting with`file://`). This default repository for artifacts will be used as the default location for Microcks to resolve relative dependencies.
...
## 2. Import content via Importer
...
Another way to add new Services or API mocks is to schedule an Importer Job in Microcks. We think it’s actually the best way to achieve continuous, iterative and incremental discovery of your Services and APIs. The principle is very simple: you save your artifact file to the Git repository of your choice (public or private), and Microcks will periodically check whether changes have been applied and whether new mock or service definitions are present in your artifact. The nice thing about using Importer is that external files referenced in the target artifact will be automatically resolved for you.

- `Imported` means that the job has been successfully imported on a previous run. Otherwise,`Last import errors` will be displayed with a pop-up showing the last error,

urls.content:
Microcks can have multiple artifacts (one`primary` and many`secondary`) mapping to one API definition. The`primary` one will bring API or Service and operation metadata and examples. The`secondary` ones will only enrich existing operations with new non-conflicting requests/responses and event samples.
...
A typical illustration of this may be using an OpenAPI specification as a`primary` one and then bringing one (or many) additional Postman collections to provide examples or test constraints.
...
In that case, Microcks is first fed with an OpenAPI file to get the main identification and structure information about the API or Service. This allows Microcks to initialize its internal metamodel for the discovered API. Then, Microcks will load the secondary artifacts and try to merge new non-conflicting information into the preexisting internal metamodel. The merging process is based on a compound key: the API name + version.
...
If not explicitly identified as`primary` or`secondary,` the default is to consider an imported artifact as the primary one. Microcks will simply ignore a`secondary` artifact if it doesn’t match any existing API name + version.
...
For specific types of APIs and protocols, loading multiple artifacts for the same API definition may be necessary. Typically, when a single artifact is not able to handle a comprehensive set of examples, we need to rely on`secondary` artifacts to provide those examples.
...
It is then mandatory to use multiple artifacts in Microcks for GraphQL, gRPC and Swagger v2 defined APIs as the`primary` artifacts that provide the structure are not able to hold complete examples (yes, even Swagger v2 doesn’t allow complete examples 😉)
...
Also, note that multiple artifacts for one API definition don’t necessarily involve different specifications and file formats! The merging process in Microcks is generic, so you can use the same format multiple times. For example, you may want to use an OpenAPI specification as a`primary` one and apply some overlay by managing examples into other OpenAPI files.
...
One specific case of the merging process - that can be used in combination with any other artifact as a`primary` one - relates to the Microcks APIMetadata format. When importing such artifacts as secondary ones, the merging process involves the metadata of the API or Service and not the examples or tests, as illustrated below:

An emerging use case is that some people may have a single OpenAPI file containing only base/simple examples but manage complementary/advanced examples using, for example, a Postman Collection.

The basic spec for a Dapr HTTPEndpoint resource

The `HTTPEndpoint` is a Dapr resource that is used to enable the invocation of non-Dapr endpoints from a Dapr application.

## Format

apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
kind: HTTPEndpoint
metadata:
  name: <NAME>  
spec:
  baseUrl: <REPLACE-WITH-BASEURL> # Required. Use "http://" or "https://" prefix.
  headers: # Optional
  - name: <REPLACE-WITH-A-HEADER-NAME>
    value: <REPLACE-WITH-A-HEADER-VALUE>
  - name: <REPLACE-WITH-A-HEADER-NAME>
    secretKeyRef:
      name: <REPLACE-WITH-SECRET-NAME>
      key: <REPLACE-WITH-SECRET-KEY>
  clientTLS:
    rootCA:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: <REPLACE-WITH-SECRET-NAME>
        key: <REPLACE-WITH-SECRET-KEY>
    certificate:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: <REPLACE-WITH-SECRET-NAME>

    privateKey:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: <REPLACE-WITH-SECRET-NAME>
        key: <REPLACE-WITH-SECRET-KEY>
scopes: # Optional
  - <REPLACE-WITH-SCOPED-APPIDS>
auth: # Optional

```

    21	
    22	The inspected order-flow system confirms the relevant behavior:
    23	
    24	- both `order-extractor` and `order-loader` use both services;
    25	- both components retain the client packages' default Dapr app IDs;
    26	- the framework calls `POST /status` and `POST /commit` on the idempotency service;
    27	- the framework calls `POST /events` with structured CloudEvents to trigger or resolve business incidents;
    28	- each component already carries local `HTTPEndpoint` resources with the production app IDs as `metadata.name` values;
    29	- those endpoints currently target locally hosted real services with their databases, messaging, migrations, and Dapr sidecars.
    30	
    31	The existing component overlay gives the SystemHost a clean substitution point: generated resources replace component-local resources with the same `metadata.name` when staging each sidecar's effective Dapr resource set.
    32	
    33	Dapr resolves a named `HTTPEndpoint` before app-ID discovery. A development resource named `idempotency-service` therefore satisfies an unchanged invocation of `/v1.0/invoke/idempotency-service/method/status` while forwarding it to Microcks.
    34	
    35	## Goals
    36	
    37	- Make platform-service dependencies visible in the topology.
    38	- Preserve existing integration code, client configuration, and service invocation paths.
    39	- Scope each generated mock endpoint to the components that declared the dependency.
    40	- Keep development substitutions separate from the environment-independent system topology.
    41	- Run one lightweight Microcks instance for all declared OpenAPI mocks.
    42	- Keep mock behavior stateless and contract-backed in the first version.
    43	- Preserve deterministic generation and the existing component-overlay model.
    44	- Fail before integration startup when a declared mock cannot be imported or addressed.
    45	
    46	## Non-goals
    47	
    48	- Deploying the real platform services.
   187	- `IDevelopmentDefinition`
   188	- `DevelopmentBuilder`
   189	- an immutable development manifest
   190	- development-definition discovery
   191	- validation of mock declarations and artifacts
   192	
   193	Discovery rules:
   194	
   195	1. The assembly must still contain exactly one `ISystemDefinition`.
   196	2. The assembly may contain zero or one concrete `IDevelopmentDefinition`.
   197	3. The system topology is built before the development definition.
   198	4. The development builder receives the validated topology so it can reject unknown or unused service references.
   199	5. No development definition means no generated service mocks and no Microcks resource.
   200	
   201	The separate development type keeps generated or regenerated system declarations focused on topology and lets local configuration evolve independently.
   202	
   203	## OpenAPI contract handling
   204	
   205	The development manifest records the service app ID and resolved artifact path. Contract inspection extracts:
   206	
   207	- OpenAPI version;
   208	- `info.title`;
   209	- `info.version`.
   210	
   211	The development tooling supports the OpenAPI versions supported by the pinned Microcks release. Missing or unreadable identity fields fail validation.
   212	
   213	Microcks URLs are built in one internal abstraction from the imported identity. SystemHost authors do not encode Microcks paths or title escaping.
   214	
   215	The first order-flow mock contracts are deliberately narrow overlays matching actual client traffic rather than copies of the full upstream API documents.
   216	
   217	### Idempotency mock
   218	
   219	Required operations:
   220	
   221	```text
   222	POST /status → 200
   223	{"action":"Proceed","reason":"NoPreviousData"}
   224	
   225	POST /commit → 200 with an empty body
   226	```
   227	
   228	The mock always allows processing and accepts every commit. It does not retain state.
   229	
   230	### Business-incident mock
   231	
   232	Required operation:
   233	
   234	```text
   235	POST /events → 202 with an empty body
   236	Content-Type: application/cloudevents+json
   237	```
   238	
   239	The same operation accepts triggered and resolved structured CloudEvents. The mock does not persist or expose incidents.
   240	
   241	Each operation includes the OpenAPI examples and Microcks associations required to produce a response, including `x-microcks-refs` where a bodyless response needs an explicit request-example association.
   245	Generation accepts the validated topology and optional development manifest. It emits one `HTTPEndpoint` for each mocked service.
   246	
   247	Conceptually:
   248	
   249	```yaml
   250	apiVersion: dapr.io/v1alpha1
   251	kind: HTTPEndpoint
   252	metadata:
   253	  name: idempotency-service
   254	spec:
   255	  baseUrl: http://localhost:8585/rest/<encoded-title>/<encoded-version>
   256	scopes:
   257	- order-extractor
   258	- order-loader
   259	```
   260	
   261	Generation rules:
   262	
   263	- `metadata.name` is the service app ID.
   264	- `spec.baseUrl` is derived from the imported OpenAPI identity.
   265	- `scopes` contains exactly the service's consumers, sorted ordinally.
   266	- Output is deterministic and one resource is emitted per mocked service.
   267	- An unmocked service emits no `HTTPEndpoint`; normal Dapr discovery or a component-local resource remains in effect.
   268	- A generated endpoint replaces a component-local endpoint with the same `metadata.name` during staging.
   269	- Mock resources are part of the local generation profile only and must not appear in production Kubernetes output.
   270	
   271	The current `generate` command emits local-run artifacts. When a development definition exists, its generated endpoints are included so command output and Aspire staging use the same generated truth.
   272	
   273	## Aspire lifecycle
   274	
   275	The Aspire backend starts Microcks only when at least one mock is declared.
   276	
   277	```mermaid
   278	flowchart LR
   279	    C[Discover and validate topology] --> D[Discover and validate development definition]
   280	    D --> G[Generate Dapr resources]
   281	    D --> M[Start one Microcks instance]
   282	    M --> I[Import OpenAPI artifacts]
   283	    I --> V[Verify imported service identities]
   284	    G --> S[Stage per-component Dapr overlays]
   285	    V --> R[Mark mock backend ready]
   286	    S --> A[Start scoped integration sidecars and apps]
   287	    R --> A
   288	```
   289	
   290	Lifecycle requirements:
   291	
   292	1. Microcks uses one pinned image version and one fixed host endpoint known to generated Dapr resources.
   293	2. Container health is necessary but not sufficient; readiness also requires every declared artifact to be imported and addressable.
   294	3. Only components consuming a mocked service depend on Microcks readiness.
   295	4. Their Dapr sidecars are held before startup until Microcks and contract import are ready.
   296	5. Sidecar recovery uses the same aggregate backend-readiness gate.
   297	6. Scheduled components use the same readiness gate on initial and subsequent starts.
   298	7. Import or verification failure stops the run with the service app ID and artifact path in the error.
   299	8. The Aspire dashboard exposes Microcks as one infrastructure resource.
   300	
   301	The fixed port is checked before startup and produces a focused error when unavailable. Port configurability is deferred until there is a demonstrated conflict that cannot be handled operationally.
   302	
   303	## CLI behavior
   304	
   305	### `check`
   306	
   307	- Validates the system topology.
   308	- Discovers and validates the optional development definition.
   309	- Verifies artifact existence and OpenAPI identity without starting Microcks.
   310	
   311	### `graph`
   312	
   313	- Includes service usage in the environment-independent topology graph.
   314	- Does not include development mock paths or Microcks details.
   315	
   316	A component entry lists its used service app IDs, and the graph's resource projection lists each service and its consumers.
   317	
   318	### `generate`
   319	
   320	- Generates the existing local Dapr resources and runtime configuration.
   321	- Includes development `HTTPEndpoint` resources when a development definition exists.
   322	- Does not start Microcks or import artifacts.
   323	
   324	### `run`
   325	
   326	- Performs all checks above.
   327	- Starts Microcks, imports and verifies contracts, stages generated endpoints, and then starts consumers.
   328	
   329	`Program.cs` remains unchanged because both backends continue discovering definitions from the SystemHost assembly.
   330	
   331	## Validation
   332	
   335	- Service app IDs must be valid DNS-1123 labels.
   336	- A component cannot use the same service more than once.
   337	- Service consumers must be declared topology components.
   338	- A service app ID cannot collide with a topology component app ID.
   339	- Service resources must have at least one consumer by construction.
   340	
   341	### Development validation
   342	
   343	- At most one development definition may exist.
   344	- A mocked service must occur in the built topology.
   345	- A service may have at most one mock declaration.
   346	- A mock artifact path must resolve within or beneath the SystemHost directory; escaping through `..` is rejected.
   347	- The artifact must exist, be readable, and contain a supported OpenAPI document with non-empty title and version.
   348	- Two different mocked services cannot accidentally resolve to the same Microcks service identity unless explicit aliasing is designed later.
   349	- A development definition may leave a used service unmocked; existing Dapr discovery or component-local resources remain valid resolution mechanisms.
   350	
   351	Validation messages identify the component or service app ID and the conflicting declaration. No new public diagnostic-code scheme is introduced by this design.
   352	
   353	## Compatibility and migration
   354	
   355	The feature is additive:
   356	
   357	- integration source code does not change;
   358	- client package registration does not change;
   359	- platform-service source code does not change;
   360	- production app IDs do not change;
   361	- existing component-local Dapr resources remain valid for standalone runs;
   362	- SystemHosts without service declarations or development definitions behave as before.
   363	
   364	For order-flow, generated mock endpoints use the same names as the existing local endpoints. The established overlay rule replaces those files only during SystemHost runs. Standalone component runs continue targeting the real local services until a separate standalone-development design is adopted.
   365	
   366	## Testing strategy
   367	
   368	### Core topology tests
   369	
   370	- Every component builder supports fluent `.Uses`.
   371	- Usage materializes deterministic component edges and service resources.
   372	- Duplicate usage and app-ID collisions fail validation.
   373	- Graph serialization includes services and consumers without development data.
   374	
   375	### Development discovery tests
   376	
   377	- Zero or one development definition is accepted.
   378	- Multiple definitions fail with their type names.
   379	- Unknown, unused, duplicate, missing, escaping, and malformed artifacts fail clearly.
   380	- OpenAPI title and version are extracted from supported 3.0 and 3.1 documents.
   381	
   382	### Generation tests
   383	
   384	- Exact `HTTPEndpoint` YAML snapshots cover name, base URL, escaping, scopes, and ordering.
   385	- Unmocked services produce no endpoint.
   386	- Generated endpoints replace component-local resources by `metadata.name` during staging.
   387	- Repeated generation is byte-identical.
   388	
   389	### Aspire model tests
   390	
   391	- No mocks means no Microcks resource or readiness dependency.
   392	- Multiple mocks share one Microcks resource.
   393	- Only consumers wait for Microcks.
   394	- Consumer sidecars are gated on contract-import readiness.
   395	- Import failures prevent component startup.
   396	- Scheduled sidecar restarts retain the readiness gate.
   397	
   398	### Live compatibility test
   399	
   400	An opt-in integration test runs the published platform-service clients through real Dapr sidecars against Microcks and proves:
   401	
   402	- idempotency status deserializes to `Proceed / NoPreviousData`;
   403	- commit receives an empty `200`;
   404	- triggered and resolved structured CloudEvents receive `202`;
   405	- integration code and app-ID configuration remain unchanged.
   406	
   407	## Acceptance criteria
   408	
   409	- The order-flow SystemHost can run both components without starting either real platform service or its backing infrastructure.
   410	- Existing invocations to `idempotency-service` and `business-incident-service` succeed through Dapr without integration changes.
   411	- The generated endpoints are scoped to `order-extractor` and `order-loader`.
   412	- A valid order flows through extractor and loader with stateless idempotency responses.
   413	- A validation failure can be routed to the business-incident mock and acknowledged successfully.
   414	- Missing or invalid contracts fail before either integration starts.
   415	- SystemHosts without development mocks retain current behavior.
   416	
   417	## Alternatives considered
   418	
   440	
   441	- **Microcks URL conventions may change.** Keep URL construction in one internal abstraction and pin the Microcks version.
   442	- **OpenAPI mocks may drift from released clients.** Exercise the published clients in an opt-in Dapr/Microcks compatibility test.
   443	- **A mock may conceal a broken production operation.** Keep mocks limited to known client traffic and do not claim production-service conformance from local mock success.
   444	- **Dapr `HTTPEndpoint` remains a `v1alpha1` resource.** Pin and test the supported Dapr runtime range.
   445	- **A fixed Microcks port may collide locally.** Check it before building the Aspire graph and report a focused remediation.
   446	- **Contract import can lag behind container health.** Gate consumers on verified artifact availability, not container state alone.
   447	
   448	## Planning handoff
   449	
   450	Implementation planning should determine:
   451	
   452	- the exact public type locations and names within existing package boundaries;
   453	- the OpenAPI parsing dependency and supported document versions;
   454	- the pinned Microcks integration package and image versions from current official documentation;
   455	- the import/verification mechanism exposed by that Microcks version;
   456	- how aggregate backend readiness is represented without coupling it specifically to Redis or Microcks;
   457	- the exact topology graph wire-format evolution and compatibility policy;
   458	- whether the live Dapr/Microcks test runs in regular CI or an opt-in compatibility lane.
   459	
   460	These choices must preserve the DSL, lifecycle, scope boundaries, and observable behavior defined above.
   461

1. **Blocker — scoped mocks can erase non-consumers’ local endpoints.**  
   `docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:265-268` emits one globally generated endpoint while relying on `scopes`; `src/Intropy.Topology.Aspire/ComponentOverlay.cs:37-46` stages that endpoint into every component and replaces any same-name local resource. A component outside the declared consumer set can therefore lose its real local endpoint while receiving a mock endpoint Dapr will not load for its app ID. Stage mock endpoints only into declared consumers, and add a mixed consumer/non-consumer overlay test.

2. **High — replacement is insufficiently keyed and operates at file granularity.**  
   The design mandates replacement by `metadata.name` alone (`docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:268,386`), matching `ComponentOverlay.cs:25-49`. A generated `HTTPEndpoint` can delete a different resource kind with the same name; duplicate local names leave one undeleted; and replacing the first resource in a multi-document YAML deletes unrelated resources in that file. Parse resources and replace by `(apiVersion, kind, metadata.name)`, or explicitly reject multi-document files and duplicate identities before staging.

3. **Blocker — import verification can pass while required operations are unusable.**  
   Validation extracts only OpenAPI version, title, and version (`docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:203-213`), and readiness verifies imported service identities (`:282-298`). A contract missing `/commit`, lacking a response association, or returning the wrong status can pass both gates and fail on the first integration request. Readiness must black-box invoke every declared mock operation through Microcks, asserting status, body, and content type before releasing consumers.

4. **High — scheduled runs can bypass backend readiness.**  
   The design requires the same gate on every scheduled start (`docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:296-297`), but `ComponentScheduler.TriggerAsync` only starts/waits for the sidecar when it is startable (`src/Intropy.Topology.Aspire/Scheduling.cs:141-166`). If Microcks becomes unavailable while the sidecar remains running, the next cron or **Run now** trigger starts the app without any backend check. Inject aggregate readiness into the scheduler and await it at the beginning of every consumer trigger, regardless of sidecar state.

5. **High — examples do not establish the promised “accept every request” behavior.**  
   `docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:228-241` claims all commits and both incident forms are accepted, but specifies only examples and `x-microcks-refs`. Dynamic idempotency keys, timestamps, incident data, or a `Content-Type` containing parameters may select no matching response under version-dependent Microcks dispatch rules. Pin an explicit body-independent dispatcher for these stateless operations and test multiple randomized payloads, both event forms, and realistic media-type headers.

6. **High — the SystemHost-relative artifact root is undefined operationally.**  
   Paths are declared relative to the SystemHost directory, but discovery begins from an assembly (`docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:193-205`), and current Aspire discovery occurs before builder creation establishes `AppHostDirectory`. `check` or `generate` invoked from a parent directory, published output, or a test runner can therefore resolve identical declarations differently. Define an explicit root passed to discovery, canonicalize paths including symlinks, and test arbitrary working directories and published assemblies.

7. **High — `generate` produces local-run resources whose backend it explicitly does not provide.**  
   `docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:271,318-322` writes endpoints targeting `localhost:8585` but neither starts Microcks nor imports contracts. Staging that generated output outside `run` replaces a working local endpoint with a dead destination. Require an explicit development-mock flag/profile, or generate a companion backend/import manifest and clearly reject unsupported direct execution.

8. **Medium — CLI failure semantics do not cover new development errors.**  
   The design promises clear pre-start failures (`docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:298,305-309,351`), while current `check` catches only `TopologyValidationException` and `generate` has no command-boundary exception handling (`src/Intropy.Topology.Generation/IntropyGenerate.cs:41-53,182-197`). Parser, file I/O, discovery, and import failures can escape as unhandled exceptions. Specify consistent exit codes and normalized diagnostics for all verbs, including service ID and artifact path without stack traces by default.

9. **Medium — the fixed-port decision prevents concurrent hosts and contains a startup race.**  
   `docs/designs/platform-service-development-mocks.md:292,301` only checks whether the port is free; it does not reserve it. Parallel SystemHosts or tests cannot coexist, and another process can claim the port after the check. Allocate or configure the Aspire endpoint and derive run-time endpoint YAML from the allocated port; test concurrent hosts. Preserve deterministic `generate` output via an explicit port option rather than a process-global constant.
